### CHAPTER ONE.

->*The Journey.*<-

In the eleventh year of the reign of *Abdul Hamid* <note>Abdul Hamid I (reigned 1774–1789), Sultan of the Ottoman Empire</note>, son of *Ahmed*, Emperor of the *Turks*; at the time when the *Nogai Tatars* <note>original: "Tartares-Nogaïs" — a nomadic Turkic people then living in the northern Black Sea region</note> were driven out of the *Crimea*, and when a Muslim prince, of the blood of *Genghis Khan*, became the vassal and the guard of a Christian woman and queen (*) <note>This refers to Catherine the Great of Russia, who annexed Crimea in 1783, making the last Khan, Sahin Giray, her dependent</note>;

I was traveling in the *Ottoman Empire*, and I traversed the provinces which were once the kingdoms of *Egypt* and *Syria*.

---

(*) That is to say, in 1784. The reader is requested not to lose sight of this date. *See the notes at the end of the volume.*

<summary>Volney establishes the historical setting of his work, beginning his travels through the Ottoman provinces of Egypt and Syria in 1784, amidst the shifting power dynamics between the Turks and the Russian Empire.</summary>
<keywords>Abdul Hamid I, Ottoman Empire, Crimea, Nogai Tatars, Genghis Khan, Catherine the Great, Egypt, Syria, historical cycles, 1784</keywords>

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page follows the traveler’s arrival in the Levant. It shifts from broad historical context to the traveler's personal observations of the suffering of the people and the physical decay of the land, leading him toward the specific destination of Palmyra.</meta>

### CHAPTER I.

Focusing all my attention on what concerns human happiness in a social state <term>social state: the organized condition of humans living together in a society, as opposed to a state of nature</term>, I entered cities and studied the customs of their inhabitants; I entered palaces and observed the conduct of those who govern; I went out into the countryside and examined the condition of those who work the land; and seeing everywhere nothing but robbery and devastation, nothing but tyranny and misery, my heart was weighed down with sadness and indignation.

Every day I found on my path abandoned fields, deserted villages, and cities in ruins. Often I came across ancient monuments, the remains of temples, palaces, and fortresses; columns, aqueducs, and tombs: and this sight turned my mind toward the contemplation of past ages, and stirred grave and profound thoughts in my heart.

And I arrived at the city of *Hems* <note>modern-day Homs, Syria</note>, on the banks of the *Orontes* <note>a major river in the Levant</note>; and there, finding myself close to the city of *Palmyra*, located in the desert, I resolved to see for myself its much-praised monuments; and, after three days of walking through arid solitudes, having crossed a valley fil- <note>The original French "rem-" likely completes to "remplie" (filled/full)</note>

## CHAPTER II.

->*Meditation.*<-

Here, I said to myself, here there once flourished an opulent city: here was the seat of a powerful empire. Yes! These places, now so deserted, were once animated by a living multitude within their walls; an active crowd circulated through these routes that are today solitary. Within these walls where a mournful silence now reigns, the noise of the arts and the cries of joy and celebration resounded incessantly: these piled-up marbles formed orderly palaces; these fallen columns adorned the majesty of temples; these collapsed galleries marked out the public squares. There, for the venerable <note>original: "respectables"—in this 18th-century context, it implies something deserving of deep respect or religious awe.</note> duties of their worship, and for the touching cares of their livelihood, a numerous people flocked together: there, an industry that created enjoyments <note>The author refers to the manufacturing of luxury goods and comforts that defined "civilized" life during the Enlightenment.</note> summoned the riches of all climates; and one saw the purple of *Tyre* <note>Tyre, in modern Lebanon, was world-famous in antiquity for its rare and expensive purple dye made from sea snails.</note> exchanged for the precious thread of *Serica* <note>original: "la Sérique"—The land of the Seres, the ancient Greco-Roman name for China, referring to the source of silk.</note>; the soft fabrics of *Cashmere* for the sumptuous carpets of *Lydia* <note>An ancient kingdom in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey) renowned for its wealth and craftsmanship.</note>; the amber of the *Baltic* for Arabian pearls and perfumes; the gold of *Ophir* <note>A legendary port mentioned in the Bible, famous for its gold; its exact location remains a mystery of the ancient world.</note> for the tin of *Thule* <note>A semi-mythical land in the far North (perhaps Scandinavia or the Shetland Islands), representing the outermost edge of the known world to the ancients.</note> (a).....

In the infancy of nations, when men still lived in forests, all subject to the same needs, all endowed with the same faculties, they were all nearly equal in strength; and this equality was a circumstance fruitful in advantages for the composition of societies: through it, each individual finding himself independent of every other, no one was the slave of another, and no one had the idea of being a master. ### CHAPTER X.

### GENERAL CAUSES OF PROSPERITY, etc.

...the character; but various circumstances combined to temper the disorder, and to make it a necessity for governments to be just.

In effect, as the States were initially weak and had to fear external enemies, it became important for the leaders not to oppress their subjects: by diminishing the *interest* <term>interest: in this context, the personal stake or "buy-in" a citizen has in the survival and success of their nation.</term> of the citizens in their government, they would have diminished their *means of resistance*; they would have facilitated foreign invasions, and for the sake of superfluous pleasures, compromised their own existence.

Internally, the character of the people repelled tyranny. Men had formed long-standing habits of independence; they had too few needs, and too present a sense of their own strength.

As the States were compact <note>original: *resserrés*. Moreover, since every man was a property owner and a farmer, no one had any need to sell himself, and the despot would have found no mercenaries.

### CHAPTER X.

If, then, dissensions arose, they were from family to family, from faction to faction, and interests were always shared by a great number: the troubles were, without a doubt, more intense; but the fear of foreigners calmed these discords. # C H A P T E R X I.

## *General causes of revolutions and the ruin of ancient States.*

However, greed <note>original: "cupidité." In the context of Enlightenment philosophy, this term refers to an unrestrained desire for wealth or power at the expense of others, which Volney identifies as the primary source of social conflict.</note> had stirred up a constant and universal struggle among men; which, by incessantly driving individuals and societies toward reciprocal invasions, occasioned successive revolutions and a recurring agitation.

And first, in the savage and barbarian state of the earliest humans, this audacious and ferocious greed taught plundering, violence, and murder; and for a long time, the progress of civilization was slowed by it.

When afterwards societies began to form, the effect of bad habits passing into laws and governments corrupted their institutions and their purpose; and there were established arbitrary and artificial rights, which depraved the ideas of justice and the morality of peoples.

And so, by these simple and natural driving forces <note>original: "mobiles" — In Volney’s materialist philosophy, these are the basic impulses of self-preservation and the pursuit of pleasure/avoidance of pain that drive all human action.</note> was the fate of ancient States governed; through such a series of linked and consistent causes and effects, they rose or fell according as the ***physical laws of the human heart*** <note>Volney suggests that human behavior and the development of societies follow natural, observable laws just like physics, rather than being determined by divine providence.</note> were observed or violated: and in the successive course of their changes, a hundred different nations, a hundred empires alternately humbled, powerful, conquered, and overturned, have repeated for the earth these instructive lessons.... # CHAPTER XII.

...who had lost their principles; your leaders were experienced, your soldiers battle-hardened and disciplined; the spoils of war stirred their passion; bravery was rewarded; cowardice and lack of discipline were punished; and all the mechanisms <note>original: "ressorts" — literally "springs," referring to the psychological motivations or driving forces of human behavior.</note> of the human heart were set in motion. Having become wealthy, you split yourselves apart for the sake of sharing and enjoyment; and disorder crept into every class of your society. The Sultan, intoxicated by his own grandeur, forgot the true purpose of his duties; and all the vices of arbitrary power <term>arbitrary power: authority exercised by a ruler without the restraint of laws or a constitution, based solely on their own will.</term> began to grow. Finding no obstacles to his whims, he became a depraved being; a man both weak and prideful, he pushed the people away from him, and the voice of the people no longer instructed or guided him. Ignorant, yet flattered, he neglected all...

# CHAPTER XIII.

...sion... <note>This syllable completes the word "passion" from the final sentence of the previous page.</note> O man who despairs of the human race <note>original: "genre humain"</note>, upon what deep calculation of facts and reasoning have you established your sentence? ->THE GREAT OBSTACLE TO IMPROVEMENT.<-

...ly struck my mind. Looking out over the globe, I saw it divided into twenty different systems of worship: each nation has received or created for itself opposing religious opinions; and each, attributing truth exclusively to itself, wishes to believe all others are in error. ## CHAPTER XVII.

### *Universal Basis of All Right and All Law.*

Then the men chosen by the people to seek out the true principles of morality <note>In this context, "morality" (French: *morale*) refers to a secular system of ethics derived from human nature and observation rather than religious decree.</note> and reason proceeded toward the sacred object of their mission; and after a long examination, having discovered a universal and fundamental principle, they said to the people: "Behold, we have found *the primordial basis, the physical origin of* *all justice and all right*." <note>Volney suggests that rights are not abstract concepts but are rooted in the physical reality of human biology and the natural world.</note>

> "Whatever may be the active power, the moving cause <note>This "active power" or "moving cause" is a deistic way of referring to a creator or the laws of nature without using specific religious titles like "God."</note> that governs the universe; having given to all men the same organs, the same sensations, the same needs, it has, by this very fact, declared that it gave to them all the same rights to the use of its gifts, and that all men are equal in the order of nature.

> "Secondly, since it has given to each person sufficient means to provide for their exis— <note>The word is truncated in the original: *existence*.</note>

tence, it clearly follows that it <note>The "active power" or "moving cause" mentioned on the previous page, representing Nature or a Creator.</note> has constituted them all as independent of one another, that it created them *free*; that none is subject to another; that each is the *absolute owner of his own being*.

(*) The words themselves trace this connection: for *equilibrium*, *equity*, and *equality* <note>original Latin: "*æqui-librium*", "*æquitas*", "*æqua-litas*"</note> are all from the same family; and the idea of the physical equality of the scales is the prototype for all the others.

# CHAPTER XIX.

->*General Assembly of the Peoples.*<-

Thus spoke the legislators; and the multitude, seized by that impulse <note>original: "mouvement"</note> which any reasonable proposition initially inspires, having applauded, the tyrants, left without support, remained confounded.

This multitude reminded me of the enameled meadows of the Nile and the Euphrates, when after the rains or the flooding, millions of flowers spring up on every side; at other times, by its murmur and its movement, it represented to me the innumerable swarms of locusts which come in spring to cover the plains of the *Hauran* <note>A volcanic plateau in southwestern Syria, known in the 18th century for its fertile but volatile environment.</note>.

Meanwhile, once the various groups had taken their places and a profound silence had followed the roar of the multitude, the legislators spoke: “Leaders and doctors of the people! <note>The term "doctors" here refers to "Doctors of the Law" or learned theologians and scholars, rather than medical practitioners.</note> You see how, until now, nations living in isolation have followed different paths; each believes it follows the path of truth; and yet, if there is only one truth, and opinions are contradictory, it is quite evident that someone is in error. Now, if so many men are mistaken, who will dare guarantee that he himself is not deceived? Begin, then, by being indulgent toward your disagreements and discords. Let us all seek the truth as if no one possessed it. Until this day, the opinions that have governed the earth—produced by chance, spread in the shadows, admitted without discussion, and validated by the love of novelty and imitation—have, in a sense, clandestinely usurped their power. <note>This passage reflects the Enlightenment critique of "prejudice"—ideas accepted through tradition or authority rather than through individual reason and evidence.</note> It is time, if they are well-founded, to

Then, the floor having been given, according to their position, to the first standard <note>In this context, the "standard" (*étendard*) refers to the banner or flag representing a specific religious or national group in the assembly.</note> on the left: “It is not permitted to doubt,” said the leaders, “that our doctrine is the only true one, the only infallible one. “And ours too!” cried out all the other standards; “and it is not permitted to doubt it!”

Well then! What does your conviction prove, if it changes nothing about the reality of things? Truth is one, while your opinions are diverse; therefore, many of you are mistaken. If, as is evident, people can be *convinced* <note>original: *persuadés*</note> of an error, what does human conviction prove?

If error has its martyrs, where is the seal of truth?

And besides, why are there always incomplete and insufficient miracles? Why, instead of these upheavals of nature, do you not change opinions instead? Why kill men or frighten them, instead of instructing and correcting them?

O credulous, and yet stubborn mortals! None of us is certain of what happened yesterday, or what is happening today before our very eyes; and yet we swear to what happened two thousand years ago!

Weak, and yet proud men! The laws of nature are immutable and profound, while our minds are full of illusion and fickleness;

Then a Rabbi, taking the floor, said: "As for the facts, we are the guarantors of their substance. Regarding the form and the use made of them, the case is different, and the Christians here condemn themselves by their own arguments; for they cannot deny that we are the original source from which they derive, the primitive trunk upon which they have been grafted. From this follows a peremptory <note>original: "péremptoire." In legal and philosophical terms, an argument that precludes further debate.</note> argument: either our law is from God, and then theirs is a heresy since it differs from it; or our law is not from God, and theirs falls at the same time."

"A distinction must be made," replied the Christian: "your law is from God as something *figurative* and *preparative*, but not as something *final* and *absolute*; you are but the *simulacrum* <note>original: "simulacre." In this theological context, it refers to a 'shadow' or 'type'—a symbolic representation that points toward a later, greater truth.</note> of which we are *the reality*."

It was therefore on the upper banks of the Nile, and among a people of the black race <note>This is a famous and controversial passage for the 18th century; Volney argued, based on his own travels and the appearance of the Sphinx, that the founders of ancient Egyptian civilization were of African descent.</note>, that the complicated system of the *worship of the stars* was organized, considered in their relationship with the productions of the earth and the labors of agriculture; and this first worship, characterized by their adoration under their *natural forms* or *attributes*, was a simple progression of the human mind: but soon the multiplicity of the objects of their relationships, of their reciprocal actions, having complicated the ideas and the signs which represented them, there occurred a confusion as bizarre in its cause as it was pernicious in its effects.

### §. III.

->*Third system. Worship of symbols, or idolatry.*<-

From the moment the agricultural people turned an observant eye toward the stars, they felt the need to distinguish individual stars or groups and to give each its own proper name, so as to understand one another when designating them. However, a great difficulty arose in this pursuit: for on one hand, the celestial bodies, being similar in form, offered no special characteristics by which they might be named; on the other hand, the burgeoning and impoverished language of the time had no expressions for so many new and *metaphysical* <note>Volney uses the term "metaphysical" here to describe abstract concepts that lack a direct, tangible physical form, requiring early humans to invent a new vocabulary for the invisible laws of nature.</note> ideas. The usual driver of genius, *necessity*, knew how to overcome everything. Having noticed that during the annual revolution, the renewal and periodic appearance of terrestrial productions were constantly associated with the *rising* or *setting* of certain stars, and with their position relative to the sun—the fundamental point of all comparison—the mind, through a natural mechanism, linked in its thought those terrestrial and celestial objects which were linked in fact; and applying to them

Thus again; he <note>Referring to the "ancient laborer" or early astronomer mentioned on the previous page.</note> called "rings" and "serpents" the figured path of the orbits of the stars and planets (51); and such was the general method of naming all the stars, and even the planets taken in groups or individually, according to their relationship to rural and terrestrial operations, and according to the analogies that each nation found there with agricultural labors and with the objects of its climate and its soil.

From this process, it resulted that lowly and earthly beings entered into association with the superior and powerful beings of the heavens; and this association grew tighter every day through the very constitution of language and the mechanism of the mind. People would say, through a natural metaphor:

"The bull sows the seeds of fertility upon the earth (in the spring); he brings back abundance and the creation of (nourishing) plants. The lamb (or ram) delivers the heavens from the malevolent spirits of winter; he saves the world from the serpent (emblem of the rainy season), and he restores the reign of good (of summer, the season of all enjoyment); the scorpion pours its venom upon the earth, and spreads disease and death, etc. and thus for all similar effects."

This language, understood by everyone, persisted at first without any disadvantage; but, with the passing of time, once the calendar had been established, the common people—who no longer had a need to observe the heavens—lost sight of the original motive behind these expressions. Their *allegory* <note>In this context, allegory refers to the use of animal names to represent star clusters or seasons.</note>, which remained in everyday use, became a fatal pitfall to understanding and reason. Accustomed to associating the ideas of the *models* with their *symbols*, the mind eventually confused the two. Thus, those same animals that human thought had once transported to the heavens descended back to earth; but in this return, dressed in the livery of the stars, they arrogated to themselves the celestial attributes and imposed themselves upon their own creators.

Then the people, believing they saw their *gods* near at hand, addressed their prayers to them more easily. They asked the *ram* of their own flock for the influences they expected from the *celestial ram* <note>The constellation Aries, which marked the spring equinox and the return of life.</note>; they prayed to the *scorpion* not to spread its venom upon nature; they revered the *crab* of the sea, the *beetle* <term>scarabée: The dung beetle, which the Egyptians associated with the sun and rebirth.</term> of the silt, the *fish* of the river; and, through a series of flawed but interconnected analogies, they became lost in a labyrinth of consistent absurdities.

This was the origin of that ancient and bizarre *worship of animals*; this was the path by which—

### CHAPTER XXII.

Thus, having first said that the sun *surmounted*, or got the better of twelve *animals* <note>This refers to the twelve signs of the Zodiac, from the Greek *zōidiakos*, meaning "circle of little animals."</note>, it was later believed that it *killed*, *fought*, or *tamed* them; and from this was fashioned the historical life of *Hercules* (*).

Having said that it *regulated* the time of labor, of sowings, and of harvests; that it *distributed* the *seasons* and occupations; that it *traversed* various climates; that it *ruled* over the earth, etc., it was taken for a *legislating* king, for a *conquering warrior*; and from this were composed the histories of *Osiris* <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and fertility, whose myths of death and rebirth mirror the solar cycle.</note>, of *Bacchus* <note>Also known as Dionysus; a god of the vine whose travels and triumphs were often interpreted as solar allegories.</note>, and of their like.

Having said that a planet *entered* into a *sign*, people turned their *conjunction* <note>The meeting of two celestial bodies in the same area of the sky.</note> into a *marriage*, an *adultery*, or an *incest* (55): having said that it was *hidden* or *buried*, because it returned to the *light* and rose again in *exaltation* <note>In ancient astrology, "exaltation" is the specific sign where a planet's influence is considered to be at its strongest.</note>, it was portrayed as *dead*, *resurrected*, *taken up to heaven*, etc.

A second cause of confusion was the material figures themselves, by which thoughts were first depicted, and which, under the name of hiero- <note>The text likely continues as "hieroglyphics."</note>

*glyphs* or *sacred characters* <note>The word "hieroglyph" comes from the Greek *hieros* (sacred) and *glyphein* (to carve).</note>, were the first invention of the mind. Thus, to warn of the flood and the need to protect oneself from it, they had painted a *skiff*, the *ship Argo* <note>The *Argo Navis* was an ancient southern constellation; in this context, it is linked to the agricultural signals related to the rising of the Nile</note>: to designate the *wind*, they had painted a *bird's wing*: to specify the *season* or the *month*, they had painted the migratory bird, the insect, or the animal that appeared at that time: to express *winter*, they painted a *pig* or a *serpent*, which delight in *damp places*; and the combination of these figures had *agreed-upon* meanings as phrases and words (* 56). But as this meaning carried nothing fixed or precise in itself; as the number of these figures and their combinations became excessive and overtaxed the memory, it first resulted in confusion and false explanations. Then, genius having invented the simpler art of applying signs to sounds—which are limited in number—and of painting speech instead of thoughts, *alphabetic writing* caused *hieroglyphic paintings* to fall into disuse; and, day by day, their forgotten meanings gave rise to a multitude of illusions, ambiguities, and errors.

Finally, a third cause of confusion was the civil organization of ancient States. Indeed, when peoples began to devote themselves to **agriculture**, the formation of the **rural calendar** <note>Also known as an almanac, these calendars were vital for survival, telling farmers when to plant and harvest based on the positions of the stars.</note> requiring continuous **astronomical observations**, it became necessary to appoint certain individuals tasked with watching for the appearance and setting of certain **stars**; to warn of the return of the **flood**, of certain winds, of the rainy season, and of the proper time to sow each kind of grain: these men, by reason of their service, were exempt from common labor, and society provided for their maintenance. In this position, solely occupied with observation, they did not delay in grasping the great **phenomena of nature**, even penetrating the secret of several of its operations: they knew the path of the **stars** and **planets**; the correlation of their phases and their returns with the products of the earth, and the movement of **vegetation**; the **medicinal** or nourishing **properties** of fruits and plants; the interplay of the elements and their reciprocal affinities. ### §. IX.

### §. XI.

Such also were the promulgators of the *sepulchral doctrine of the Samaneans* <note>Samaneans: A term used by ancient Greek and later European writers to refer to Shramanas, the wandering ascetics of India, including Buddhists and Jains.</note>, who, upon the foundations of *metempsychosis* <term>Metempsychosis: The philosophical concept of the transmigration of the soul, or reincarnation into a new body after death.</term>, raised the misanthropic system of *renunciation* and *deprivations*; who, laying down as a principle that the *body* is nothing but a *prison* where the *soul* lives in *impure constraint*, that *life* is but a *dream*, an *illusion*, and the *world* a place of passage to a *further Fatherland*, to a *life without end*, placed virtue and perfection in *absolute immobility*, in the *destruction of all feeling*, in the *abnegation* of physical organs, and in the *annihilation* of the entire *being*: from which resulted the *fasts*, *penitences*, *mortifications*, *isolation*, *contemplations*, and all the practices of the deplorable delirium of the *Anchorites* <note>Anchorites: Religious recluses who withdraw from society to live a life of prayer and penance.</note>.

### §. XII.

->*Brahminism, or the Indian System.*<-

Such, finally, were the founders of the Indian system, who, refining upon Zoroaster’s <note>Zoroaster was the ancient Persian prophet who founded Zoroastrianism, centered on the struggle between light and dark.</note> two principles of *creation* and *destruction*, introduced an *intermediate* one: that of *preservation*. Upon their distinct yet identical trinity of *Brahma*, *Shiva*, and *Vishnu* <note>The author uses the spellings Brama, Chiven, and Bichenou. These represent the Trimurti, the triple deity of supreme divinity in Hinduism.</note>, they heaped the allegories of ancient traditions and the over-refined subtleties of their metaphysics.

These were the materials that, for many centuries, existed scattered throughout Asia, until a fortuitous course of events and circumstances—along the banks of the Euphrates and the Mediterranean—brought them together into new combinations.

But you yourselves, replied the simple men, with all your knowledge <note>original: "science"—in this 18th-century context, "science" refers to formal, scholarly learning or theology rather than the modern natural sciences</note>, you do not agree! Of what use is it to possess it?

That offends God, said the doctors. Where is the proof of it? said the simple men. — *In our books*, replied the doctors.

## CHAPTER XXIV.
### Solution to the problem of contradictions.

And the legislators, speaking once more, said:

O Nations! we have heard the debates of your opinions; and the disagreements that divide you have given us much to reflect upon, and present several questions for us to clarify and propose to you.

First, considering the diversity and the opposition of the beliefs to which you are attached, we ask you upon what grounds you base your conviction: is it by a reasoned choice <note>original: *choix réfléchi*</note> that you follow the banner of one prophet rather than another? Or rather, have you received them only by the chance of birth, and through the power of habit and education? Now, from this first fact flows a second, equally clear and worthy of note. Because you agree on what you know with certainty, it follows that you are *discordant* only regarding what you do not know well, regarding that of which you are not sure; that is to say, *that you dispute, that you quarrel, that you fight for what is uncertain, for what you doubt.* <note>The author is pointing out the irony that humanity reserves its greatest violence for subjects it understands the least.</note> **O** men! is this wisdom?

In all ages, the custom of the East was to call the palaces and the houses of the great *gates*, for the reason that the principal luxury of these dwellings consists of the single *gate* <note>Original: "porte." In many Middle Eastern cultures, the "Gate" refers to the seat of power or the royal court, as in the "Sublime Porte" of the Ottoman Empire</note> that provides entrance from the street into the courtyard, at the back of which the buildings are always recessed. Homer undoubtedly knew all this; but poets do not provide commentary, and their readers desire the marvelous.

This city of *Thebes*, today Luxor, reduced to the condition of a miserable village, has left behind astonishing traces of magnificence. One can find the details in the plates of Norden <note>Frederic Louis Norden (1708–1742), a Danish explorer known for his drawings of Egyptian monuments</note>, in Pococke <note>Richard Pococke (1704–1765), an English traveler and bishop</note>, and in the recent voyage of Mr. Bruce <note>James Bruce (1730–1794), the Scottish explorer who reached the source of the Blue Nile</note>.

# N O T E S.

These relationships provided it with a level of activity that was even greater because Lower Egypt <note>The northern region of Egypt, consisting of the Nile Delta</note>, initially marshy, was for a long time uninhabitable or sparsely populated.

As civilization grows, manners soften, and the condition of women improves, until, by another excess, they come to dominate, and then a nation is weakened and corrupted. It is remarkable that paternal authority is all the greater where the government is more despotic. China, India, and Turkey <note>In the 18th century, "Turkey" was used to refer broadly to the Ottoman Empire</note> are striking examples of this. One might say that tyrants grant themselves accomplices, and that they engage subaltern despots <term>subaltern despots: Lower-ranking or subordinate tyrants who enforce the will of a higher ruler within their own smaller spheres of influence, such as the home</term> to maintain their authority. The Romans will be cited as a counterexample; but it remains to be proven that the Romans were truly free men; and the so-rapid transition from their republican despotism to their deep enslavement under the emperors casts at least great doubt on that liberty.

Page 82. (*r*) *And to mysteriously pronounce Aúm.* This word is a sacred emblem of Divinity in the Indian religion <note>Specifically Hinduism.</note>. It must only be pronounced in secret, and without anyone hearing it. It is formed of three letters, of which the first, *a*, designates the principle of everything, the creator *Brahma*; the second, *u*, designates the preserver *Vichen-ou* <note>original: "Vichen-ou" — a French phonetic spelling of Vishnu.</note>; and the last, *m*, the destroyer who brings everything to an end, *Chiven* <note>original: "Chiven" — a French phonetic spelling of Shiva.</note>. It is pronounced as the monosyllable *ôm*, which designates the unity of these three gods. This is absolutely the same idea as that of the *alpha* and the *omega* <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, used in Christian scripture to symbolize the beginning and the end.</note>, of which the Gospel speaks.

Modern critics, even more enlightened or more attentive than those of antiquity, have found in *Genesis* in particular signs of its composition upon the return from the captivity <note>The Babylonian Captivity (c. 597–539 BCE), a period in Jewish history during which a large number of Judeans were forced to live in Babylon.</note>; but the principal proofs have escaped them. I propose to gather them in an analysis of *Genesis*, and I will demonstrate therein, among other things, that Chapter X, which deals with the alleged generations of the so-called man *Noah*, is a true geographical table of the world known to the Hebrews at the time of the captivity, which has as its limits *Greece* or *Hellas* to the west, the *Caucasus* to the north, *Persia* to the east, and *Arabia* and Upper Egypt to the south. All the alleged characters from *Adam* to *Abraham*, or his father *Terah* <note>original: *Tharé*</note>, are mythological beings, stars, constellations, or countries: *Adam* is the constellation *Boötes* <note>A constellation in the northern sky, often depicted as a herdsman.</note>; *Noah* is *Osiris*, *Xisuthrus* <note>The hero of the Sumerian flood myth, analogous to Noah.</note>, *Janus*, *Saturn*—that is to say, Capricorn, or the celestial spirit who opened the year. By the very admission of the *Chronicle of Alexandria* <note>A 7th-century Byzantine universal chronicle of the world.</note>, page 85, *Nimrod* was supposed by the Persians to be their first king, having invented the art of hunting; and he had been transported to the heavens, where he was seen under the name of *Orion*: thus it is with the ten generations, which are the same as those of the Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia.</note> in the works of Berosus and Syncellus <note>Berosus was a Babylonian priest and historian (3rd century BCE); George Syncellus was a Byzantine chronicler (9th century CE) who preserved fragments of Berosus's work.</note>.

*six periods of time*. These periods are what Zoroaster <note>The ancient Iranian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism.</note> calls the *thousands of God*, or of the light—that is to say, the six months of summer. In the first, say the Persians, God created (put in order) the *sky*; in the second, he created the *waters*; in the third, the *earth*; in the fourth, the *trees*; in the fifth, the *animals*; and in the sixth, *man*: precisely like the book of *Genesis*. In the first thousand, God made the heaven and the earth; in the second, the firmament; in the third, the sea and the waters; the sun in the fourth, the moon, and the plants; in the fifth, the soul of the birds, animals, and reptiles; in the sixth, man. The *Asiatic Miscellany* <note>original: "Mélanges asiatiques," referring to the journal *Asiatick Researches*.</note> is hardly known in Europe; and one must be a scholar in the Oriental genre to have heard of the likes of Jones, Wilkins, Halhed, etc. <note>Sir William Jones, Charles Wilkins, and Nathaniel Brassey Halhed were pioneering British scholars who first translated Sanskrit texts into English.</note> As for Indian theological books, those we possess to this day are the *Bhagavad Gita* <note>original: "Bhagouet guîta"</note>, the *Ezour-Vedam* <note>A work once thought to be an ancient Veda, later discovered to be an 18th-century Jesuit manuscript intended for missionary use.</note>, the *Bhagavata Purana* <note>original: "Bagavadam"</note>, and fragments of several Shastras <note>original: "chastres"; Hindu scriptures concerning law, ritual, and discipline.</note> published with the *Bhagavad Gita*. These books are to the Indians what the *Old* and *New Testament* are to Christians, the *Quran* <note>original: "Qoran"</note> to Muslims, the *Sad Dar* and the *Zend-Avesta* to the Parsis <note>Followers of Zoroastrianism.</note>, etc. Considering what they all contain, I have sometimes asked myself what truth the human race would lose if a new Omar <note>A reference to the Caliph Umar and the legend of the burning of the Library of Alexandria; the author suggests that destroying these religious texts would result in no loss of actual knowledge.</note> burned them; and I have not been able to discover a single one: I call the chest where I keep them Pandora's box.

This is why Homer calls him the father and king of men and gods. (Diodorus, Book 1, Section 1.)

Among the theologians, says Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer known for his commentary on the 'Dream of Scipio' and his 'Saturnalia.'</note>, *Jupiter* <note>original: "You-piter."</note> is the soul of the world: hence the words of Virgil: *Muses, let us begin with Jupiter: all is full of Jupiter* <note>original Latin: "Ab Jove principium Musae: Jovis omnia plena." (91) *At the end of the alleged six thousand years.* We have already seen, in note 29, this tradition existing among the Tuscans <note>The Etruscans of ancient Italy.</note>; it was spread among most peoples, and it reveals to us what should be thought of all these alleged creations and ends of the world, which are only the beginnings and ends of astronomical periods imagined by astrologers. That of the year, or solar revolution, being the simplest and most perceptible, served as a model for all the others, and its comparison gave rise to very bizarre ideas. Such is that of the four ages of the world among the Indians <note>Referring to the *Yugas* in Hindu cosmology.</note>: originally, these four ages were only the four seasons; and as each of them was under the alleged influence of a planet, it bore the name of the metal attributed to that planet: thus spring was the age of the sun or of gold; summer, the age of the moon or of silver; autumn, the age of Venus or of copper; and winter, the age of Mars or of iron. Later, when astrologers had invented their "great years" of 25 and 36 thousand years, which were intended to bring all the celestial bodies back to the same starting point—to a general conjunction <note>A "conjunction" occurs when multiple planets or celestial bodies appear in the same area of the sky.</note>—the ambiguity of terms introduced an ambiguity of ideas, and it was easy to mistake the thousands of years of revolution...

solar revolutions, which were in reality only markers of celestial signs and duration: thus, all these ideas of creation about which people have troubled themselves so much are reduced to hypothetical calculations of astronomical periods; and it is because the beginnings of these periods were taken, and the fictional moment of conjunctions at the opening of various seasons, that the *creation of the world* was supposed to have occurred sometimes in the spring, sometimes at the solstice, depending on the time at which each people began their year. Among the Egyptians, it was at the summer solstice; therefore, the departure of the spheres occurred, according to them, at the first sign of Cancer <note>original: "Macrobe, Somn. Scip." refers to Macrobius, a 5th-century Latin author whose *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* was a vital source for ancient cosmology and astrology.</note>. Among the Persians, it was originally in the spring at the first sign of Aries; and from this comes the opinion of the early Christians that the world was created in the spring. This opinion could not fail to be that of Genesis; and it is remarkable that it does not have the world created by the God of Moses <insert>Yahweh</insert>, but by the *elohim* or *gods* in the plural, that is to say, by the *angels* or *spirits*, according to the usual sense of the Hebrew books; and if one observes that the root of *elohim* signifies *strong* and *powerful*, and that the Egyptians called their *decans* <term>Decans: groups of stars used in ancient Egyptian astronomy to divide the 360-degree zodiac into 36 parts of 10 degrees each, each ruled by a specific "chief" or deity.</term> *strong and powerful chiefs*, while attributing creation to them, one will find that Genesis said word for word that the world was created by the *decans*—by those same spirits that Mercury raised against Saturn, according to Sanchuniathon <note>Sanchuniathon was a legendary Phoenician author whose works, preserved in fragments, describe a complex mythology where celestial bodies were personified as gods.</note>, and who were named *Elohim*.

...what is a magician in the sense that the common people give to this word? It is a man who, through words and gestures, claims to act upon supernatural beings, and to force them to descend at his voice, to obey his orders. This is what all the ancient priests have done, what those of all the idolaters still do, and what, on our part, earns them the name of magicians. But when a Christian priest claims to make God descend from heaven, to fix him upon a piece of leavened bread <note>The author uses "levain" (leaven), though the Roman Catholic host is typically unleavened; this may be a deliberate rhetorical choice to de-mystify the Eucharist as mere fermented dough.</note>, and to make souls pure and in a state of grace with this talisman, what is he doing himself, if not an act of *magic*? And what difference is there between him and a Tartar Shaman <note>A practitioner from the indigenous religions of Central and Northern Asia.</note>, who invokes spirits, or an Indian Brahmin, who makes *Vishnu* <note>The principal deity in Hinduism, the Preserver.</note> descend into a vessel of water to drive away evil spirits? Yes! everywhere the identity of the sacerdotal spirit <note>The spirit or mindset of the priesthood.</note> is complete; everywhere there is the affectation of an *exclusive privilege*, the faculty of moving the powers of *nature* at one's will; and this claim is so direct an attack on the right of equality of all men, that on the day when the people become consistent, they will forever abolish this sacrilegious kind of *nobility*, which was the root and the model for profane nobility.

...would be to place side-by-side in columns the analogous or contrasting features of belief and superstition among all peoples. Another kind of superstition from which it would be equally useful to cure them <note>The "them" refers to the general public or "the people" mentioned later in the text.</note> is the exaggerated respect for the great <term>the great: *les grands*, a term used to describe the high-ranking nobility and those in positions of power</term>; and, for this purpose, it would suffice to write the details of the private lives of kings and princes. What would it be if we had the sequel? If the people saw openly all the depravities and miseries of these kinds of idols, they would no longer be tempted to desire their false pleasures, the deceptive appearance of which torments them and prevents them from enjoying the much truer happiness of their own condition.
